headline: An estimated 37.2% of adults in the City of Rochester feel lonely at least some of the time, against 28.3% to 32.6% in 18 of Monroe County's 20 suburban towns. Of the 25 census tracts where 40% or more of adults are estimated to be lonely, 23 are in the city.

blocks.heading: What the data shows
paragraphs: Loneliness is common across Monroe County: CDC estimates that 32.5% of adults feel lonely at least some of the time, roughly one in three. It is most common in the City of Rochester, at an estimated 37.2%.

Most suburban towns sit well below the city, between 28.3% and 32.6%. The lowest are Mendon (28.3%), Perinton (28.5%) and Rush (29.0%). Two towns are closer to the city: Sweden (36.0%) and Henrietta (35.1%).

Neighborhood by neighborhood, estimates range from 26.2% in a tract in Perinton to 47.6% in a tract in Sweden. Inside the city they range from 27.7% to 43.4%. 23 of the 25 tracts at 40% or more are in the city; the other 2 are in Henrietta and Sweden.

The highest estimates of all are for the three college campuses the Census counts as their own places (Census names): Nazareth College (46.2%), Rochester Institute of Technology (45.5%), St. John Fisher College (44.9%).

Among the county's towns, the city also has the highest estimated share of adults who lack the social and emotional support they need (28.7%, against 20.1% in Brighton and 21.7% in Irondequoit). It ties with Sweden for the highest share with frequent mental distress (18.8%, against 12.9% in Brighton and 14.7% in Irondequoit).
The gaps hold after CDC adjusts for differences in age: Rochester's age-adjusted loneliness estimate is 36.4%, against 31.0% in Brighton and 32.9% in Irondequoit.

Diagnosed depression follows a different pattern. The share of adults ever told they have depression differs much less: 22.3% in the city, 20.2% in Brighton, 22.0% in Irondequoit and 21.9% countywide.

blocks.heading: What this means
items: Feeling lonely is common here. About one in three Monroe County adults reports feeling lonely at least some of the time, so it is not unusual and not a personal failing.
Loneliness is not only a city experience. Even the least lonely neighborhood in the county has an estimated 26.2% of adults who feel lonely at least some of the time.
Loneliness and depression are different measures, and in this data they follow different patterns across the county.
Ruzicka Psychology offers [individual therapy](/specialties/individual-therapy) in Rochester and virtually across New York. Local support lines are listed on our [resources page](/resources).

blocks.heading: How we built the map
paragraphs: Estimates: CDC PLACES, 2025 release, which estimates the share of adults with each measure in every county, place and census tract from the 2023 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS). Loneliness counts adults who say they feel lonely always, usually or sometimes. Lack of social and emotional support counts adults who say they get the support they need sometimes, rarely or never. Frequent mental distress counts adults who say their mental health was not good on 14 or more of the past 30 days. Figures are crude prevalence (the actual share of adults) unless marked age-adjusted.

Towns: each census tract is assigned to the town (or the City of Rochester) that contains its Census internal point, using Census 2020 boundaries. A town's figure is the average of its tracts' estimates, weighted by the number of adults in each tract.

Places: CDC also publishes estimates for Census places. Some places, such as Rochester, Brighton and Irondequoit, cover a whole town or city. Others, such as the villages and the Greece and Gates Census-designated places, cover only part of a town, so their figures can differ from the town averages.

blocks.heading: What these estimates cannot tell you
paragraphs: These are model-based estimates, not counts from a survey of each neighborhood. CDC predicts survey answers for each area from BRFSS survey responses and the characteristics of the people who live there, such as age, sex, and race and ethnicity. Two areas with similar populations will get similar estimates even if their residents feel differently.

Each estimate has a likely range (95% confidence interval), and most of them overlap. Rochester's range for loneliness (32.7% to 41.5%) overlaps with the ranges for 16 of the 17 other places in the county that are not college campuses; only the Village of Pittsford's range sits entirely below it. The city-suburb pattern is consistent on the map and across loneliness, support and distress, but the gap between the city and any single suburb is less certain than the single numbers suggest.
Loneliness was asked in an optional BRFSS module, so the estimates rest on fewer survey answers than common measures.
The data shows where loneliness is more common. It does not show why, and it does not say anything about what helps.
